content:
Dexter Morgan is back on the hunt — and this time, he is not the only killer working New York. Dexter: Resurrection season 2 premiered Friday, October 30, on Paramount+ Premium, with the premiere episode, "Risky Business," arriving at 3:01 a.m. ET. The return lands as the Dexter franchise marks its 20th anniversary.

Michael C. Hall returns as Dexter Morgan, the serial killer with a code who targets other killers. Season 2 picks up three years after the events of season 1, still set in New York City, where Dexter's son Harrison has also taken up what the show calls the family business. The new season runs 10 episodes, with new installments arriving every Friday on Paramount+ Premium and the finale scheduled for Friday, January 1, 2027. The premiere also airs on Showtime on Sunday, November 1, at 8:00 p.m. ET.

Two new killers anchor the season. Brian Cox joins as Don Framt, known as the New York Ripper, and Dan Stevens joins as Lucas Stark, known as the Five Borough Killer, a killer who strikes across the city's boroughs to terrorize New York. Per Paramount, Dexter finds himself caught between the two killers while battling an unexpected enemy of his own: a mid-life crisis.

Showrunner Clyde Phillips framed that crisis around a long-running thread in the character. "In his own weird midlife crisis way, one of the things that Dexter has always wanted is recognition," Phillips told Entertainment Weekly in September 2026, as reported by People. Early critical response is positive but still thin: Dexter: Resurrection season 2 debuted with an 86% score on Rotten Tomatoes based on just six reviews, compared with a near-perfect 95% for season 1, according to Screen Rant — a small early sample, not a settled verdict.

Analysis: A Familiar Killer, A More Crowded Hunting Ground

The season 2 setup changes Dexter's usual math. In the original series, Dexter was often the hidden predator in a city that did not know he existed. Now the show gives New York two headline killers of its own, which puts Dexter in an unusual position: he is hunting, but he is also competing for the same dark attention he has always craved. That mid-life-crisis framing may be the season's sharpest idea — after 20 years, the question is no longer whether Dexter can kill and get away with it, but whether being seen, even by other killers, is what he wanted all along. If the weekly rollout holds its early promise, the slow drip of episodes could work in the show's favor, giving each new threat room to unsettle before the next one arrives.
